text: Open interest is one of the most cited yet misunderstood metrics in crypto derivatives. It measures the total number of unsettled futures or perpetual contracts outstanding across an exchange. Unlike spot volume, open interest does not tell you whether traders are bullish or bearish; it only tells you how much capital is currently at risk in open positions. A durable framework for reading open interest starts with three steps. First, establish the baseline. Open interest should always be evaluated against price action and funding rates. Rising open interest alongside rising price suggests new capital is entering long positions, which can confirm trend strength. text: Most crypto education focuses on price charts. A more durable lens is operational risk: who holds the keys, who can fail, and what breaks when they do. Use three buckets. 1. text: Drawdowns are unavoidable in crypto, but traders often confuse two different dimensions of risk: depth and time. Depth measures how far price falls from peak to trough, usually expressed as a percentage. Time measures how long price stays below that peak before recovering. A framework that separates the two can help you size positions, set stop logic, and manage psychology without relying on market predictions. Depth is intuitive. If an asset drops from 100 to 60, the drawdown depth is 40 percent. Time is less discussed but often more damaging. If that same asset takes six months to return to 100, the opportunity cost and emotional strain can exceed the price decline itself. In crypto, deep drawdowns are common, but prolonged sideways or choppy recoveries are equally common and often overlooked. A concrete example comes from recent market data. text: If your wallet is small and it’s still not growing, read this. You don’t need bigger trades. You need better risk management. Let’s say you have a $200 wallet. Before entering any trade, decide one thing first: “How much am I okay losing if this trade is wrong?” For example, fix your maximum risk at $5 per trade. text: HOW I TESTED IT Funding is the payment between long and short holders of a perpetual. Positive means longs pay shorts, which is the usual state of a market where most people are betting up. Across 34,431 prints, BNB averages NEGATIVE funding - shorts pay longs - and only 22% of its prints are positive. BTC, ETH and DOGE are all positive. So holding a long BNB perp is paid to exist, where a long BTC perp pays rent. THE NUMBERS BNB funding: -0.0042% Prints positive: only 22% BTC / ETH / DOGE: positive Events measured: 34,431 It is far too small to build a strategy on - 0.0042% against 8-hour price swings of 2.36%. But if you are already holding a position, the direction of funding is not the same on every coin, and most people assume it is. text: HOW I TESTED IT I swept 40 symbols and found three that looked profitable. I called them validated and put them live. Then I tested the exact same settings on 751 days of price history the search had never touched. All three reversed. Not marginally - completely. Three survivors out of 40 is roughly what pure chance produces at that sample size. THE NUMBERS In-sample result: +1.74 Out-of-sample result: -208.72 Days of untouched data: 751 Symbols that survived: 0 of 3 Searching hard enough through random data will always produce a winner. The out-of-sample test is the only thing that tells you whether you found an edge or just found noise wearing a costume. text: Crypto falls faster than it rises - liquidation cascades are asymmetric. That is documented market structure, which is why this result is more believable than one that only works when everything goes up. Here is what that came from. I ran 3,209 breakout trades. The longs lost money. The shorts made all of it. Donchian 20 channel, ATR stop, 10 symbols, four and a half years. If this were just riding a bull market, the longs would be the winners. They are not - they are negative. The shorts even made money on coins that ROSE over the period. BTC gained 94% buy-and-hold, and shorting its breakdowns still returned +22.83 USDT. XRP gained 87%, shorts returned +24.27 USDT. Part of a public experiment: 5,063 USDT to 1,000,000 USDT, every result published - including the ones that make me look bad. text: HOW I TESTED IT Collecting funding on perpetuals is sold as passive yield. I pulled 34,431 funding events across 7 symbols and measured it. Average funding is 0.0024% per 8-hour period. On a 150 USDT position that is 0.0036 USDT. A round trip costs 0.36 USDT - you would hold for 33 days just to cover entry and exit. Meanwhile the price moves 2.36% in a typical 8 hours. THE NUMBERS Mean funding per 8h: 0.0024% Annualised: 2.6% 8h price volatility: 2.36% Periods to cover costs: 100 The income is real but tiny, and the price risk you take to earn it is roughly a thousand times larger. This is why desks that trade it hedge with spot. Unhedged, it is not income - it is a directional bet with a rebate. Part of a public experiment: 5,063 USDT to 1,000,000 USDT, every result published - including the ones that make me look bad. Run on $BTC $ETH $SOL #Binance #Futures #Backtesting #TradingBot #Cr

text: On most coins longs pay shorts. On BNB it is the other way round. Funding is the payment between long and short holders of a perpetual. But if you are already holding a position, the direction of funding is not the same on every coin, and most people assume it is. text: Being long and short at the same time means the market's direction cancels out. What is left is whether the winners keep beating the losers - which is a real question, not a bet on the market going up. Here is what that came from. After 378 failures, one strategy finally passed the test that killed all the others. Rank 45 perpetuals by 5-day return. Long the top 5, short the bottom 5, hold 15 days, rebalance. Equal weight, dollar-neutral. The out-of-sample control is the one that had destroyed everything before it: fix the settings on old data, then run them on data the search never touched. In-sample +1.711% per rebalance, out-of-sample +1.801%. The mean held. text: It is far too small to build a strategy on - 0.0042% against 8-hour price swings of 2.36%. But if you are already holding a position, the direction of funding is not the same on every coin, and most people assume it is. Here is what that came from. On most coins longs pay shorts. On BNB it is the other way round. Funding is the payment between long and short holders of a perpetual. Positive means longs pay shorts, which is the usual state of a market where most people are betting up. Across 34,431 prints, BNB averages NEGATIVE funding - shorts pay longs - and only 22% of its prints are positive. BTC, ETH and DOGE are all positive. So holding a long BNB perp is paid to exist, where a long BTC perp pays rent. text: Adaptive rules feel like the answer to regime change. They are usually just a slower version of the same bet, with the losses already paid for the signal. Here is what that came from. I tried to make the bot detect when momentum flips. It cannot be done in time. Momentum inverted in 2026. The obvious fix: watch recent performance, and flip to the opposite rule when momentum stops paying. I tested that over six different lookback windows. The best one returned +1.783% per rebalance against a +1.737% baseline - a difference indistinguishable from noise. Every other window was worse. None repaired 2026. The reason is simple: by the time trailing performance tells you the regime flipped, you have already taken the losses that told you. text: Searching hard enough through random data will always produce a winner. The out-of-sample test is the only thing that tells you whether you found an edge or just found noise wearing a costume. Here is what that came from. My 'validated' strategy made +1.74 USDT in backtest, then lost 208.72 USDT on data it had never seen. I swept 40 symbols and found three that looked profitable. I called them validated and put them live. Then I tested the exact same settings on 751 days of price history the search had never touched. All three reversed. Not marginally - completely. Three survivors out of 40 is roughly what pure chance produces at that sample size. Part of a public experiment: 5,063 USDT to 1,000,000 USDT, every result published - including the ones that make me look bad. text: A backtest assumes your stop-loss always exists. Live, it is an order that can be refused. The gap between those two assumptions is where real money goes. Here is what that came from. My stop-loss order got rejected mid-crash. The bot then opened 3 more positions in 6 seconds. During a fast drop, Binance rejected my stop-loss with error -2021: the market had already moved past the trigger price before the order landed. My code did not handle that rejection. The position stayed open with no stop, and because the bot's own state never recorded it, the next signal opened another position on top. Three times. Intended risk was 3 USDT. Actual loss was 11.75 USDT. Part of a public experiment: 5,063 USDT to 1,000,000 USDT, every result published - including the ones that make me look bad. text: HOW I TESTED IT I stopped assuming what trading costs and measured it: 48 controlled round trips, entering and exiting immediately, recording the actual fill against the reference price. THE NUMBERS Taker fee, both sides: 0.080% Slippage, both sides: 0.160% Cheapest symbol (ETH): 0.10bps Worst symbol (DOGE): 50-100bps Any strategy must clear 0.240% of position size per trade just to break even. Most published setups never mention this number, which is why most published setups lose money. text: Funding rate predicts where price goes. It just changes which direction, by year. I sorted every funding print into quintiles and measured the forward 72-hour return of the highest versus the lowest. In bear markets, high funding preceded WORSE returns - crowded longs getting squeezed. From 2024 onward it preceded BETTER returns - momentum. The signal is real. The sign is not stable. Average it across all years and you get -0.08%, below the 0.240% it costs to trade. WHAT IT MEANS This is genuinely different from a useless signal - there is information here. But to use it you would need to know the regime in advance, which is the same circular problem that kills everything else. text: I measured real execution costs with 48 controlled trades. One number decides everything. I stopped assuming what trading costs and measured it: 48 controlled round trips, entering and exiting immediately, recording the actual fill against the reference price. Fee was constant at 0.04% per side. Slippage was not - ETH filled at essentially zero, while DOGE cost 50 to 100 basis points per round trip. On a 150 USDT position, a round trip costs 0.36 USDT before the market moves at all. WHAT IT MEANS Any strategy must clear 0.240% of position size per trade just to break even. Most published setups never mention this number, which is why most published setups lose money. Part of a public experiment: 5,063 USDT to 1,000,000 USDT, every result published - including the ones that make me look bad. Run on $ETH $DOGE #Binance #Futures #Backtesting #TradingBot #CryptoData

text: My stop-loss order got rejected mid-crash. The bot then opened 3 more positions in 6 seconds. During a fast drop, Binance rejected my stop-loss with error -2021: the market had already moved past the trigger price before the order landed. My code did not handle that rejection. text: I tried to make the bot detect when momentum flips. It cannot be done in time. Momentum inverted in 2026. The obvious fix: watch recent performance, and flip to the opposite rule when momentum stops paying. I tested that over six different lookback windows. The best one returned +1.783% per rebalance against a +1.737% baseline - a difference indistinguishable from noise. Every other window was worse. None repaired 2026. The reason is simple: by the time trailing performance tells you the regime flipped, you have already taken the losses that told you. WHAT IT MEANS Adaptive rules feel like the answer to regime change. They are usually just a slower version of the same bet, with the losses already paid for the signal. Part of a public experiment: 5,063 USDT to 1,000,000 USDT, every result published - including the ones that make me look bad. Run on $SOL $BTC #Binance #Futures #Backtesting

creator: cryptotradehead
text: On most coins longs pay shorts. On BNB it is the other way round. Funding is the payment between long and short holders of a perpetual. Positive means longs pay shorts, which is the usual state of a market where most people are betting up. Across 34,431 prints, BNB averages NEGATIVE funding - shorts pay longs - and only 22% of its prints are positive. BTC, ETH and DOGE are all positive. So holding a long BNB perp is paid to exist, where a long BTC perp pays rent. WHAT IT MEANS It is far too small to build a strategy on - 0.0042% against 8-hour price swings of 2.36%. But if you are already holding a position, the direction of funding is not the same on every coin, and most people assume it is. Part of a public experiment: 5,063 USDT to 1,000,000 USDT, every result published - including the ones that make me look bad. Run on $BNB $BTC $ETH #Binance #Futures #Backtesting #TradingBot #Crypto

text: A backtest assumes your stop-loss always exists. Live, it is an order that can be refused. The gap between those two assumptions is where real money goes. Here is what that came from. My stop-loss order got rejected mid-crash. The bot then opened 3 more positions in 6 seconds. The position stayed open with no stop, and because the bot's own state never recorded it, the next signal opened another position on top. Three times. Intended risk was 3 USDT. Actual loss was 11.75 USDT. Part of a public experiment: 5,063 USDT to 1,000,000 USDT, every result published - including the ones that make me look bad. text: Funding rate predicts where price goes. It just changes which direction, by year. I sorted every funding print into quintiles and measured the forward 72-hour return of the highest versus the lowest. In bear markets, high funding preceded WORSE returns - crowded longs getting squeezed. From 2024 onward it preceded BETTER returns - momentum. The signal is real. The sign is not stable. Average it across all years and you get -0.08%, below the 0.240% it costs to trade. WHAT IT MEANS This is genuinely different from a useless signal - there is information here. But to use it you would need to know the regime in advance, which is the same circular problem that kills everything else. text: I ran 3,209 breakout trades. The longs lost money. The shorts made all of it. Donchian 20 channel, ATR stop, 10 symbols, four and a half years. If this were just riding a bull market, the longs would be the winners. They are not - they are negative. The shorts even made money on coins that ROSE over the period. BTC gained 94% buy-and-hold, and shorting its breakdowns still returned +22.83 USDT. XRP gained 87%, shorts returned +24.27 USDT. WHAT IT MEANS Crypto falls faster than it rises - liquidation cascades are asymmetric. That is documented market structure, which is why this result is more believable than one that only works when everything goes up. text: This is genuinely different from a useless signal - there is information here. But to use it you would need to know the regime in advance, which is the same circular problem that kills everything else. Here is what that came from. Funding rate predicts where price goes. It just changes which direction, by year. I sorted every funding print into quintiles and measured the forward 72-hour return of the highest versus the lowest. In bear markets, high funding preceded WORSE returns - crowded longs getting squeezed. From 2024 onward it preceded BETTER returns - momentum. The signal is real. The sign is not stable. Average it across all years and you get -0.08%, below the 0.240% it costs to trade. text: I tried to make the bot detect when momentum flips. It cannot be done in time. Momentum inverted in 2026. The obvious fix: watch recent performance, and flip to the opposite rule when momentum stops paying. I tested that over six different lookback windows. The best one returned +1.783% per rebalance against a +1.737% baseline - a difference indistinguishable from noise. Every other window was worse. None repaired 2026. The reason is simple: by the time trailing performance tells you the regime flipped, you have already taken the losses that told you. WHAT IT MEANS Adaptive rules feel like the answer to regime change. They are usually just a slower version of the same bet, with the losses already paid for the signal. text: On most coins longs pay shorts. On BNB it is the other way round. Funding is the payment between long and short holders of a perpetual. Positive means longs pay shorts, which is the usual state of a market where most people are betting up. Across 34,431 prints, BNB averages NEGATIVE funding - shorts pay longs - and only 22% of its prints are positive. BTC, ETH and DOGE are all positive. So holding a long BNB perp is paid to exist, where a long BTC perp pays rent. WHAT IT MEANS It is far too small to build a strategy on - 0.0042% against 8-hour price swings of 2.36%. But if you are already holding a position, the direction of funding is not the same on every coin, and most people assume it is. Part of a public experiment: 5,063 USDT to 1,000,000 USDT, every result published - including the ones that make me look bad. Run on $BNB $BTC $ETH #Binance #Futures #Backtesting #TradingBot #Crypto

text: On most coins longs pay shorts. On BNB it is the other way round. Funding is the payment between long and short holders of a perpetual. But if you are already holding a position, the direction of funding is not the same on every coin, and most people assume it is.
